The lighthouse keepers of Kestrel Rock

By Priya Sharma · 20 November 2026

Share on Social Share on Email

For two hundred years the lighthouse on Kestrel Rock was kept by families who rowed out with the spring tide and stayed until the autumn gales. The keepers wrote the weather into a ledger three times a day, and the ledgers survive in a cupboard of the harbour office.

Mara Ellison, whose grandfather kept the light until 1961, has spent the last year reading them page by page. She found storms that are still talked about in the village, and quiet weeks in which the only entry is the colour of the sea.

A life on the rock

A life on the rock was ruled by the lamp and the clock. The wick was trimmed at dusk and at midnight, the lens was polished every morning, and the brass was cleaned on Saturdays whatever the weather.

Supplies came by boat once a fortnight, and when the boat could not land the keepers lived on salted fish and the potatoes they grew in a sheltered corner of the rock.

We were never lonely, Ellison remembers her grandfather saying, because the sea was always talking.

  • Trim the wick at dusk and at midnight.
  • Polish the lens every morning.
  • Clean the brass on Saturdays.

The last keepers

The light was automated in 1961, and the last keepers rowed ashore for good on a calm morning in October. The ledgers record it in a single line.1

YearKeeper
1893Thomas Ellison
1961John Ellison

The harbour office plans to put the ledgers on show next spring, beside the lamp that was taken down when the light went electric. Visitors will be able to read the entries for the night of the great storm of 1893, when the keepers kept the light burning for thirty hours without sleep.

  1. Harbour office, ledger 14, page 202. ↩
